newsitem.title: USA: Nissan slashes prices for top-selling Altima.
newsitem.headline: Nissan slashes prices for top-selling Altima.

text.p: Nissan Motor Corp. U.S.A., trying to put some spark in its lackluster car sales, on Thursday slashed the price on 1998 models of its top-selling Altima mid-size sedan as much as 7.6 percent.

The price of a 1998 Altima GXE with automatic transmission, which accounts for most of the Altima volume, is now $18,460, including a $470 destination charge -- $1,508 below the price for a similarly equipped 1997 model with the company's value option package.
Nissan said it was cutting the prices of all four trim versions of the Altima, the Japanese automaker's best-selling vehicle in the United States last year.
The starting price for an entry level Altima XE is now $15,460 after destination charges, down from $16,319. A top-line GLW with automatic transmission is now $20,360. The car was previously $21,369.

The new Altima, featuring better handling, a quieter ride and more room than the previous version, is the second-generation of the car, first introduced in 1992. It will go on sale July 10, said Thomas Eastwood, vice president for the Nissan Division.

Eastwood, speaking at an Automotive Press Association lunch meeting, said Nissan expects the new Altima to generate total U.S. sales of 170,000 during the 1998 model year. For 1996, Altima sales were 147,910. Altima's traditional annual sales volume is about 150,000.

"Since we believe consumers will respond very positively to the enhancements and the savings, we're projecting sales to increase -- even in a much more crowded market than when we introduced the original," said Eastwood.

Eastwood boasted that the Altima GXE price cut was nearly double the price cuts Toyota Motor Corp. unveiled for the 1997 model year. Nissan is able to cut Altima prices because of technology and production improvements at its Smyrna, Tenn., plant, where the car is built.
Toyota spokesman John McCandless said the company is not concerned about increased competition for its hot-selling Camry from the new Altima.
"Our biggest problem is not having enough product out there in the market," he said.

Nissan expects the Altima to help its efforts to boost Nissan division sales 20 percent over the next three years. Over the next four years, Nissan will be introducing a new vehicle every six months, said Eastwood.
Separately, Eastwood for the first time indirectly confirmed previous industry reports that Nissan plans to introduce a new small sport utility vehicle
"We haven't officially announced a compact sport/utility that's coming down the road," he said.
